Off the track: Tulane Formula Racing prioritizes access, community engagement

Eva Becker, Staff Writer
October 12, 2026
Dylan Boling
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:56
Instaread

Tulane Formula Racing is about more than motorsports; from sponsoring students’ racing licenses to bringing Hot Wheels to patients at the local children’s hospital, the club works to embed itself in both Tulane University and the New Orleans community. 

The club began as Tulane’s sports car club, founded in the 1960s and operating until the 1980s. The club later evolved into the Formula One club, which took a hiatus after Hurricane Katrina and reformed in 2021. 

Now, the club is focused on getting Tulane students involved in racing.

This is the inaugural year of the Collegiate Race Series, a national Formula One racing championship that hosts teams from over 80 colleges and universities. 

This year, Tulane’s F1 team traveled to races in Atlanta and Louisville, Kentucky, and is currently ranked sixth in the championship. 

Competition racing has a high barrier to entry. It can cost anywhere from $500 to $1,500 to get certified, with the necessary equipment costing thousands more. 

TFR tries to make racing more accessible by providing student drivers with the necessary gear — and even sponsoring racing licenses when possible. 

Carla Roozen-Briswalder, the club’s president, said the F1 club helps students through every part of the process. 

“We get them to the track. We make them go-karting to help them learn, and then we teach them manual,” Briswalder said. “When the opportunity is there with the racing school, we help them pass the test.” 

Student driver Tai Nguyen said he didn’t even have his regular driver’s license when he began learning to race with TFR. Now he’s racing competitively around the country with the team.  

“Going from that to this was surreal,” Nyugen said. “I loved every moment of it, and I hope we’re able to continue to do this.”

The club also sponsors a capstone project for engineering students, who collaborate each year to build an F1 style race car. 

Trevor Kaskade, a Tulane engineering student who worked on the project both this year and last year, said working on the car helped him refine his engineering skills.

“Being able to apply everything that I’ve learned in school … to one singular project was just really rewarding because I could see all the hours I spent studying … and taking them directly and applying them … was a really really cool experience,” Kaskade said. 

This year, the students said they hope to take their car to the annual Formula Society of Automotive Engineers contest in Michigan, where their car will be evaluated on endurance, design and functionality. 

In addition to racing and preparing for the FSAE competition, Nguyen said he enjoys the TFR’s community engagement most. 

“One of the most spectacular parts about the club is the fact that we give back to the community,” Nguyen said. “After all, I’m from New Orleans. I love being able to give back to the community that helped me get here today.”
